Abandoned but not Forgotten

Six machines. Two worlds. All still out there.

Since the 1960s, NASA has left hardware across the solar system — on the Moon, on Mars, and in deep space. Some of it finished its mission long ago. Some of it is still working. One probe is still travelling away from Earth right now.

This is their story — told by the machines themselves.

Start on the Moon → 6 chapters 2 things to try yourself Quiz + fact check at the end

Use the Next button, the page dots, the arrow keys, or swipe to turn the pages. Every chapter follows the same four steps: Meet it → Its job → Goodbye → What it still tells us.

Contents

Where shall we go first?

Our trip moves further from home on every page — from the Moon, to Mars, to the edge of the Solar System. Tap any chapter to jump straight to it.

For teachers: one chapter is one short reading session. Each chapter ends with the science it made possible, and the last page has a quiz and a full fact check with sources.

Chapter 1 · The Moon

The car that never came home

The Lunar Rover speaks

“I am a car with no roof, no doors and wire wheels — and I live on the Moon. In December 1972 I carried astronauts Gene Cernan and Harrison Schmitt around Taurus-Littrow. Then they flew home… and I stayed. I am still parked exactly where they left me.”

Meet it. The Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) was a folding, battery-electric rover. Three of them went to the Moon, on Apollo 15, 16 and 17. This last one drove about 36 km — the longest Moon drive of all.

Its job. Astronauts on foot could only explore near their lander. The rover let them visit distant craters and rocks, and carry far more Moon rock back. Its TV camera was left pointing at the lander, so people on Earth could watch the astronauts lift off for home.

Goodbye. There was no room and no fuel to bring a car home — so all three rovers were left behind, one at each landing site.

What it still tells us. The Moon has no wind, no rain and almost no atmosphere, so nothing rusts or blows away. The rovers, their tracks and the astronauts' footprints are still there — a museum with no walls, preserved by emptiness itself.

~36 kmdriven by Apollo 17's rover
3rovers left on the Moon
1972parked at Taurus-Littrow
Chapter 2 · The Moon

The mirror that still answers

Meet it. On Apollo 11, 14 and 15, astronauts placed special mirror panels on the Moon called retroreflectors. They have no batteries, no switches and no moving parts. Apollo 15's is the biggest — about 105 × 65 cm.

Its job. Scientists on Earth fire laser pulses at the mirrors. The light bounces straight back, and by timing the round trip they measure the Earth–Moon distance to within millimetres or centimetres.

Goodbye? There wasn't one. The science stations placed beside them (ALSEP) were switched off in 1977 — but the mirrors never needed power, so they are still working, more than 50 years later.

What it still tells us. Those measurements show the Moon is drifting away from Earth by about 3.8 cm every year — roughly as fast as your fingernails grow.

Try it: fire the laser

Light takes about 2.5 seconds to go to the Moon and back. Press the button and watch the pulse make the trip.

Chapter 3 · The Moon

Small things, big stories

Not everything left on the Moon is a machine. Astronauts left small, human things too — and every one has a reason. Tap an object to read its story.

Why leave things behind? Every gram mattered. To bring precious Moon rocks home, crews left behind anything they no longer needed. In total there are roughly 180 tonnes of human-made material on the Moon — and with no weather, it all stays where it was left.

Chapter 4 · Mars

The little rover that ran a marathon

Opportunity speaks

“I was built to last 90 Martian days. I lasted more than fourteen years. I found round pebbles nicknamed ‘blueberries’ that only form in water — proof that Mars was once wet. Then a dust storm covered the whole planet, the sky went dark… and I went to sleep.”

Meet it. Opportunity landed at Meridiani Planum on Mars in 2004, on a planned mission of just 90 sols (a sol is one Martian day).

Its job. It searched for signs of past water — and found them: hematite “blueberries”, evidence that liquid water once soaked the Martian ground.

Goodbye. In June 2018 a global dust storm blocked its sunlight. NASA declared the mission over on 13 February 2019 — after 5,111 sols and 45.16 km, a full marathon distance, on another planet.

Try it: how long is 5,111 sols?

Drag the slider from Opportunity's planned mission to its real one.

90 sols ≈ 0.3 Earth years Planned: 90 sols · Real: 5,111 sols (57× longer)

Bar shows progress toward the final 45.16 km marathon distance.

What it still tells us. Opportunity's twin, Spirit, is still on Mars too — it worked over 6 years before getting stuck in soft sand in 2009; its last message came in March 2010. Nothing has ever been brought back from Mars. Every robot we send stays there.

Chapter 5 · Mars

The helicopter that shouldn't have flown

Meet it. Ingenuity is a tiny helicopter — just 1.8 kg — that rode to Mars tucked under the Perseverance rover and was set down in Jezero Crater.

Its job. Mars air is about 100 times thinner than Earth's, so most people thought flying there was impossible. On 19 April 2021 Ingenuity made the first powered, controlled flight on another world.

Goodbye. It was planned for just 5 flights. It completed 72. On its final landing, on 18 January 2024, its rotor blades were damaged, and it could not fly again. It still rests in Jezero Crater.

What it still tells us. Every future Mars explorer can now have a flying scout. Ingenuity proved a whole new way to explore other worlds.

72flights (5 were planned)
1.8 kglighter than a house cat
19 Apr 2021first flight on another world

Not abandoned: Perseverance — Ingenuity's parent rover — is still working on Mars today, and so is Curiosity, which landed in 2012. Not every machine's story has ended. Some chapters are still being written.

Also resting on Mars: the Viking 1 & 2 landers (1976, the first successful Mars landings), Sojourner (1997, the first wheeled rover on Mars — planned ~7 days, active ~83 sols), and InSight (2018–2022), which listened to marsquakes until dust covered its solar panels.

Chapter 6 · Deep space

The postcards that will outlive us

Meet them. Not all discarded hardware sits still. Voyager 1 and Voyager 2, launched in 1977, are the farthest human-made objects ever — and they are still travelling, and still sending signals home.

Their job. Voyager 1 entered interstellar space on 25 August 2012; Voyager 2 — the only spacecraft ever to visit Uranus and Neptune — followed on 5 November 2018. Each carries a Golden Record: music, greetings and sounds of Earth, a postcard to anyone who might one day find it.

Goodbye? Pioneer 10, launched in 1972, was the first craft through the asteroid belt and past Jupiter. Contact was lost in January 2003, but it is still out there, drifting toward the star Aldebaran, carrying a plaque showing who sent it.

What they still tell us. Five spacecraft are now on their way out of the Solar System for good: Voyager 1 & 2, Pioneer 10 & 11, and New Horizons. They will outlive the mountains of Earth. “Abandoned” is the wrong word — they are messengers.

Your turn

Voyager carries greetings in 55 languages. If you could add one message of your own, what would it say?

Fact check — every number in this book

ObjectKey facts used
Lunar Rovers (Apollo 15–17)Apollo 17 drove ~36 km (15 ~28 km, 16 ~27 km); cameras left filming liftoff.
Retroreflectors (Apollo 11, 14, 15)Still working after 50+ years; Moon receding ~3.8 cm/year; Apollo 15 array ~105 × 65 cm; ALSEP stations switched off 1977.
Small things on the Moon6 flags (Apollo 11's fell in the liftoff blast); 96 waste bags; Armstrong's boots; Shepard's 2 golf balls (Apollo 14, 1971); Duke's family photo (Apollo 16); Scott's hammer-and-feather drop (Apollo 15); ~180 tonnes of material in total.
OpportunityPlanned 90 sols → 5,111 sols, 45.16 km; hematite “blueberries”; dust storm June 2018; mission declared over 13 Feb 2019.
SpiritPlanned 90 sols, worked >6 years; stuck 2009; last message March 2010.
Ingenuity1.8 kg; first powered flight on another world 19 Apr 2021; 5 planned → 72 flights; rotor damage 18 Jan 2024.
Still working — not abandonedCuriosity (landed 2012) and Perseverance (landed 18 Feb 2021) remain operational.
Voyager 1 & 2Launched 1977; interstellar 25 Aug 2012 (~122 AU) and 5 Nov 2018 (~119 AU); both still functioning.
Pioneer 10Launched March 1972; contact lost Jan 2003; heading toward Aldebaran, carrying the Pioneer plaque.
